title: Doubt, Emotion and the Past Subjunctive
bigQuestion: How does Spanish talk about what is uncertain, what has not happened yet, and what would happen if the world were different?

story.title: If I Could Change One Thing
story.kicker: A civics teacher asks her class to describe one change they would make to their town, and the assignment turns out to need a verb form nobody has practiced.
paragraphs: Señora Reyes teaches Spanish for heritage speakers at a high school in Aurora, west of Chicago. In March she writes one sentence on the board: "Si pudieras cambiar una cosa de tu ciudad, ¿qué cambiarías?" (If you could change one thing about your town, what would you change?) She asks the class to answer in a paragraph, in Spanish, by Friday.

Daniela starts writing right away. "Si tuviera el poder, pondría más autobuses por la noche." (If I had the power, I would put more buses on at night.) Her friend Omar reads it over her shoulder and frowns. "Tuviera? Pondría? Those aren't words we learned." Daniela shrugs. "Así lo dice mi abuela. Si yo fuera rica, si tuviéramos más tiempo…" (That is how my grandmother says it. If I were rich, if we had more time…) She has heard the forms her whole life; she has just never seen them written.

Omar tries his own. "Si puedo cambiar una cosa, cambio el parque." Señora Reyes reads it and asks, gently, whether he really can change the park. "No," he admits. "That is the point," she says. "Spanish has one way to talk about things that might really happen, and another way to talk about things that are only imagined. Your sentence says you can. Daniela's says she wishes she could."

The class spends the week on the difference. They learn that *dudo que* (I doubt that) and *no creo que* (I do not think that) push a verb into the subjunctive, while *creo que* (I think that) leaves it alone. They learn that *para que* (so that) and *antes de que* (before) always take it, and that *cuando* (when) takes it only when the moment is still in the future. And they meet a past form of the subjunctive, tuviera, fuera, pudiera, that pairs with the conditional to build the sentence on the board.

By Friday, Omar's paragraph reads: "Si pudiera cambiar una cosa, arreglaría el parque para que los niños jugaran sin miedo." (If I could change one thing, I would fix the park so that the kids could play without fear.) Every verb is in the right mood. This chapter walks the same road the class did.
story.think: In English, what is the difference between "If I have time, I will go" and "If I had time, I would go"? Which one do you say when you know you will not go?

lessons.title: Dudo que and Creo que
lessons.mainIdea: Doubt and denial trigger the subjunctive, while belief and certainty keep the indicative, so the same sentence can flip moods when no is added.
reading: Omar and Daniela disagree about the new bus schedule. Daniela says, "Creo que el autobús llega a las siete" (I think the bus arrives at seven). Omar answers, "Dudo que llegue a las siete; siempre llega tarde" (I doubt it arrives at seven; it always arrives late). Two opinions, two moods. *Creer que* expresses belief and keeps the indicative llega. *Dudar que* expresses doubt and takes the subjunctive llegue. The mood tells the listener how much the speaker trusts the claim.

The doubt group includes *dudar que* (to doubt that), *no creer que* (to not believe that), *no pensar que* (to not think that), *negar que* (to deny that), *no estar seguro de que* (to not be sure that), and *no es verdad que* (it is not true that). The certainty group includes *creer que*, *pensar que*, *estar seguro de que*, *saber que* (to know that), *es verdad que* and *es obvio que* (it is obvious that). Learn them as pairs, because most of them are the same phrase with and without no.

That pairing is the point of this lesson. "Estoy seguro de que hay un parque nuevo" (I am sure there is a new park) uses hay. "No estoy seguro de que haya un parque nuevo" (I am not sure there is a new park) uses haya. "Es verdad que la ciudad necesita más luz" (It is true the city needs more light) uses necesita. "No es verdad que la ciudad necesite más luz" uses necesite. English says the same words either way; Spanish changes the verb.

Heritage speakers often have this instinct already and can hear that "no creo que viene" sounds off. If you do not have the instinct yet, build it with a test. Ask whether the speaker is standing behind the claim or stepping away from it. Standing behind it means indicative. Stepping away means subjunctive.

words.d: to doubt that — subjunctive follows: Dudo que llegue a tiempo (I doubt it arrives on time)
to be sure that — indicative follows unless negated: Estoy seguro de que hay tiempo
it is not true that — subjunctive follows: No es verdad que sea caro (It is not true that it is expensive)
it is obvious that — certainty, indicative follows: Es obvio que necesitamos más autobuses

look.title: Two Neighbors, One Rumor
look.text: A rumor says the city will close the pool this summer. Don Ramón: Estoy seguro de que la cierran; lo leí en el periódico. (I am sure they are closing it; I read it in the paper.) Doña Clara: No creo que la cierren; siempre dicen eso. (I do not think they are closing it; they always say that.) Omar: Dudo que tengan el dinero para arreglarla. (I doubt they have the money to fix it.) Daniela: Es obvio que nadie sabe nada. (It is obvious that nobody knows anything.)
look.prompt: Mark each verb after que as indicative or subjunctive and explain the choice. Which speaker sounds most certain?

check.q: No creo que el autobús ___ (llegar) a tiempo.
check.why: No creer que expresses doubt, so the verb is the subjunctive llegue. Llega would follow creo que without no.

check.q: Which sentence keeps the indicative?
choices: Dudo que haya un parque nuevo.
No es verdad que haya un parque nuevo.
Niego que haya un parque nuevo.
Estoy seguro de que hay un parque nuevo.
check.why: Estar seguro de que shows certainty and takes the indicative hay. The other three doubt or deny and take haya.

check.q: What does "No es verdad que la ciudad necesite más luz" mean?
choices: It is true that the city needs more light.
The city does not need more light.
It is not true that the city needs more light.
I hope the city needs more light.
check.why: No es verdad que means it is not true that, and necesite is the subjunctive that follows a denial.

lessons.title: Questions, Maybe and Perhaps
lessons.mainIdea: Questions with creer can take either mood depending on what the speaker expects, and quizás and tal vez take the subjunctive when the speaker is unsure.
reading: When creer or pensar turns into a question, the speaker is no longer stating a belief. "¿Crees que el alcalde escucha a los jóvenes?" (Do you think the mayor listens to young people?) with the indicative escucha is a neutral question. "¿Crees que el alcalde escuche a los jóvenes?" with the subjunctive escuche adds a shade of doubt, as if the asker already suspects the answer is no. Both are correct. The mood lets the speaker signal an attitude without saying it.

The words *quizás* and *tal vez*, both meaning maybe or perhaps, work the same way. "Quizás llueve mañana" (Maybe it rains tomorrow) with the indicative sounds fairly confident. "Quizás llueva mañana" with the subjunctive sounds genuinely unsure. Most speakers use the subjunctive after these words most of the time, and that is the safest choice for a learner. The word *a lo mejor* (maybe) is different: it always takes the indicative, "A lo mejor llueve."

Notice that none of these sentences has two clauses. Quizás and tal vez sit in front of a single verb, the way ojalá does. That is a reminder that the subjunctive is not really about que; it is about the speaker's stance. Que is simply the most common place to see the stance change, because a main clause of wanting or doubting is usually there.

Daniela's paragraph uses one of these. "Tal vez la ciudad no tenga dinero para más autobuses, pero debería buscarlo" (Maybe the city does not have money for more buses, but it should look for it). Tenga is subjunctive because she is guessing, not reporting.

words.d: maybe, perhaps — usually followed by the subjunctive when the speaker is unsure: Quizás llueva
maybe, perhaps — like quizás: Tal vez no tenga dinero (Maybe it does not have money)
maybe — always followed by the indicative: A lo mejor llueve
the mayor — ¿Crees que el alcalde escuche? (Do you think the mayor will listen?)

look.title: Guessing About Friday
look.text: The class talks about the town meeting on Friday. Omar: Quizás vaya mucha gente. (Maybe a lot of people will go.) Daniela: Tal vez el alcalde no venga. (Maybe the mayor will not come.) Omar: A lo mejor hablan del parque. (Maybe they will talk about the park.) Daniela: ¿Crees que nos escuchen? (Do you think they will listen to us?) Omar: Creo que sí. (I think so.)
look.prompt: Which sentence uses the indicative after a maybe word, and why? What does the subjunctive in Daniela's question tell you about what she expects?

check.q: Which maybe-word is always followed by the indicative?
check.why: A lo mejor takes the indicative: A lo mejor llueve. Quizás and tal vez usually take the subjunctive, and ojalá always does.

check.q: Tal vez la ciudad no ___ (tener) dinero para el proyecto.
check.why: Tal vez with real uncertainty takes the subjunctive: tenga. Tiene is possible but sounds confident, and the speaker here is guessing.

check.q: "¿Crees que el alcalde escuche a los jóvenes?" What does the subjunctive escuche suggest?
choices: The asker doubts the mayor listens.
The question is about the past.
The mayor is the one asking.
check.why: In a question with creer, the subjunctive adds a shade of doubt. With escucha the question would be neutral.

lessons.title: Reacting to What Happens
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs of emotion such as alegrarse de que, sentir que and temer que take the subjunctive in the que clause, even when the event is real.
reading: Emotion verbs trigger the subjunctive even when the thing you feel about is a plain fact. "Me alegro de que el parque tenga luces nuevas" (I am glad the park has new lights). The lights are real. The sentence is still about my reaction, so tenga is subjunctive. This is the trigger English speakers resist the most, because in English the fact seems to matter more than the feeling. In Spanish, once the main clause reacts, the mood follows.

The common emotion triggers: *alegrarse de que* (to be glad that), *sentir que* (to be sorry that), *temer que* (to fear that), *tener miedo de que* (to be afraid that), *sorprenderse de que* (to be surprised that), *esperar que* (to hope that), *es triste que* (it is sad that), *me gusta que* (I like that), *me molesta que* (it bothers me that). Sentir has two meanings; "Siento que no puedas venir" means I am sorry you cannot come, with the subjunctive, but "Siento que va a llover" means I sense that it is going to rain, a report, with the indicative.

Daniela's paragraph about her town has several. "Me molesta que los autobuses dejen de pasar a las nueve" (It bothers me that the buses stop running at nine). "Es triste que los niños no puedan jugar en el parque de noche" (It is sad that the kids cannot play in the park at night). "Temo que nada cambie" (I fear nothing changes). Each one names a feeling, then que, then a verb in the subjunctive.

Remember the one-subject rule from the previous chapter. "Me alegro de estar aquí" (I am glad to be here) uses the infinitive, because I am glad and I am here. "Me alegro de que estés aquí" (I am glad you are here) needs que and the subjunctive, because you are here and I am the one who is glad.

words.d: to be glad that — Me alegro de que vengas (I am glad you are coming)
to be sorry that (subjunctive) or to sense that (indicative): Siento que no puedas venir / Siento que va a llover
to fear that — Temo que nada cambie (I fear nothing changes)
it is sad that — Es triste que no puedan jugar (It is sad they cannot play)
I like that — Me gusta que la gente participe (I like that people take part)

look.title: What Students Would Change (Example Survey)
look.cite: A made-up class survey of 35 students, for practice only
look.prompt: Write three reactions to these results in Spanish: one with me sorprende que, one with me alegro de que, and one with es triste que. Check every verb after que.

check.q: Me alegro de que el parque ___ (tener) luces nuevas.
check.why: Alegrarse de que is an emotion trigger, so the verb is subjunctive even though the lights are real: tenga.

check.q: Which sentence means "I am sorry you cannot come"?
check.why: Sentir que meaning to be sorry takes the subjunctive puedas. With puedes it would sound like a report, and sé que means I know.

check.q: Why does "Me alegro de estar aquí" use the infinitive?
choices: Because the same person is glad and is here
check.why: One subject means the infinitive. Me alegro de que estés aquí, with two subjects, needs que and the subjunctive.

lessons.title: So That, Before, Unless
lessons.mainIdea: Some connecting words always take the subjunctive because what follows them has not happened yet: para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que, con tal de que and en caso de que.
reading: A *conjunción* (conjunction) is a word that joins two clauses, like because, so that, or before. Some Spanish conjunctions point to something that has not happened and may never happen, and those always take the subjunctive. *Para que* (so that): "Arreglan el parque para que los niños jueguen" (They are fixing the park so that the kids will play). The playing is the goal, not yet a fact. *Antes de que* (before): "Terminan antes de que empiece el verano" (They finish before summer begins). Summer has not begun.

The full set that always takes the subjunctive: *para que* (so that), *antes de que* (before), *sin que* (without), *a menos que* (unless), *con tal de que* (provided that), and *en caso de que* (in case). Teachers sometimes group them by their first letters. "No cambian nada a menos que la gente hable" (They do not change anything unless people speak up). "Salgo sin que mis padres me vean" (I leave without my parents seeing me). "Llevo paraguas en caso de que llueva" (I bring an umbrella in case it rains).

Contrast these with conjunctions that report a reason or a result. *Porque* (because) takes the indicative: "Arreglan el parque porque los vecinos se quejaron" (They are fixing the park because the neighbors complained). The complaining happened. *Así que* (so, therefore) also takes the indicative. The difference between para que and porque is the difference between a purpose and a cause. Purpose looks forward, so it takes the subjunctive; cause looks back, so it takes the indicative.

When there is no change of subject, several of these drop que and take an infinitive: "Trabajo para ganar dinero" (I work in order to earn money), "Antes de salir, cierro la puerta" (Before leaving, I close the door). Add a new subject and the que returns with the subjunctive: "Trabajo para que mi hermano gane dinero" (I work so that my brother earns money).

words.d: conjunction — a word that joins two clauses: porque, para que, cuando, antes de que
so that — always subjunctive: para que los niños jueguen (so that the kids play)
before — always subjunctive: antes de que empiece el verano (before summer begins)
unless — always subjunctive: a menos que la gente hable (unless people speak up)
in case — always subjunctive: en caso de que llueva (in case it rains)
because — reports a cause, so it takes the indicative: porque los vecinos se quejaron

look.title: Plans for the Town Meeting
look.text: Omar's plan. Voy a hablar en la reunión para que el alcalde escuche a los jóvenes. Quiero llegar antes de que empiece, para sentarme adelante. No voy a gritar a menos que nadie me deje hablar. Llevo mis notas en caso de que me ponga nervioso. Voy porque el parque me importa. (I am going to speak at the meeting so that the mayor hears young people. I want to arrive before it starts, to sit up front. I am not going to shout unless nobody lets me speak. I am bringing my notes in case I get nervous. I am going because the park matters to me.)
look.prompt: Find the four conjunctions that take the subjunctive and the one that takes the indicative. Why does para sentarme not need que?

check.q: Arreglan el parque para que los niños ___ (jugar) sin miedo.
check.why: Para que always takes the subjunctive. Jugar keeps its stem change and adds u after g before e: jueguen.

check.q: Which conjunction takes the indicative?
check.why: Porque gives a cause that already happened, so the indicative follows. The other three point to something not yet real.

check.q: What does "No cambian nada a menos que la gente hable" mean?
choices: They change nothing because people talk.
They change nothing unless people speak up.
They change everything when people speak.
They change nothing before people speak.
check.why: A menos que means unless, and hable is the subjunctive that always follows it.

lessons.title: When, Until and As Soon As
lessons.mainIdea: Time conjunctions such as cuando, hasta que and en cuanto take the subjunctive when the event is still in the future, and the indicative when it is habitual or already happened.
reading: *Cuando* (when) is the most common conjunction in Spanish, and its mood depends on time. "Cuando llego a casa, hago la tarea" (When I get home, I do my homework) describes a habit, so it takes the indicative. "Cuando llegué a casa, hice la tarea" (When I got home, I did my homework) reports the past, also indicative. But "Cuando llegue a casa, haré la tarea" (When I get home, I will do my homework) points to a moment that has not arrived, and that pushes llegar into the subjunctive.

The same rule covers *hasta que* (until), *en cuanto* (as soon as), *tan pronto como* (as soon as), *después de que* (after) and *mientras* (while). Future and not yet real: subjunctive. Habit or past: indicative. "Esperaré hasta que termine la reunión" (I will wait until the meeting ends) uses termine. "Siempre espero hasta que termina la reunión" (I always wait until the meeting ends) uses termina. "En cuanto abran el parque, vamos a ir" (As soon as they open the park, we are going to go) uses abran.

English gives no help here. "When I get home" is the same in all three sentences, so English speakers must ask a question the language never made them ask: has this already happened, does it happen regularly, or is it still ahead? A future or a command in the main clause is the strongest clue. "Llámame cuando llegues" (Call me when you arrive) is a command about a moment still to come, so llegues is subjunctive.

Señora Reyes's class made a chart. Past: cuando llegué. Habit: cuando llego. Future: cuando llegue. The first two are indicative in different tenses. Only the third is subjunctive, and only because the arrival is still ahead. Daniela's paragraph ends with one: "Cuando yo sea alcaldesa, los autobuses van a pasar toda la noche" (When I am mayor, the buses are going to run all night).

words.d: when — subjunctive for a future moment (cuando llegue), indicative for habit or past (cuando llego, cuando llegué)
until — Esperaré hasta que termine (I will wait until it ends); indicative for habit
as soon as — En cuanto abran el parque, vamos (As soon as they open the park, we go)
as soon as — Tan pronto como llegues, llámame (As soon as you arrive, call me)

look.title: Three Versions of One Sentence
look.text: Daniela's grandmother, talking about the pool. Cuando era niña, nadaba en esa piscina todos los veranos. (When I was a girl, I swam in that pool every summer.) Ahora, cuando hace calor, me siento en la sombra. (Now, when it is hot, I sit in the shade.) Cuando la arreglen, voy a nadar otra vez. (When they fix it, I am going to swim again.) Past, habit, future: three cuando clauses, three verb forms.
look.prompt: Identify the mood and tense of the verb after each cuando. Then write your own three-sentence past, habit, future set about your own street.

check.q: Llámame cuando ___ (llegar) a casa.
check.why: The main clause is a command about a future moment, so cuando takes the subjunctive: llegues.

check.q: Which sentence describes a habit and correctly uses the indicative?
choices: Cuando llegue a casa, haré la tarea.
En cuanto abran el parque, iremos.
Cuando llego a casa, hago la tarea.
check.why: Cuando llego, hago describes what happens regularly, so both verbs are present indicative. The others point to the future.

check.q: Why is "Esperaré hasta que termine la reunión" subjunctive?
choices: Because esperar is a wish verb
Because hasta que always takes the subjunctive
Because the meeting has not ended yet
check.why: Time conjunctions take the subjunctive when the event is still ahead. With a habit, hasta que termina would be indicative.

lessons.title: Building the -ra Forms
lessons.mainIdea: The imperfect subjunctive comes from the preterite ellos form: drop -ron, add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran, with an accent on the nosotros form.
reading: The present subjunctive handles wishes and doubts about now and the future. When the main clause is in the past, or when the wish is only imagined, Spanish uses the *imperfecto de subjuntivo* (imperfect subjunctive). It has one starting point for every verb in the language: the ellos form of the preterite. That is the good news. There are no separate irregulars to learn, because every irregularity already lives in the preterite you know.

Three steps. Take the preterite ellos form of *hablar*: hablaron. Drop -ron: habla-. Add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran: hablara, hablaras, hablara, habláramos, hablarais, hablaran. Comer: comieron, comie-, comiera, comieras, comiera, comiéramos, comierais, comieran. Vivir: vivieron, viviera, vivieras, viviera, viviéramos, vivierais, vivieran. The only accent falls on the nosotros form, on the vowel just before -ramos.

Now the verbs that are irregular in the preterite. Ser and ir share fueron, so both become fuera, fueras, fuera, fuéramos, fuerais, fueran. Tener: tuvieron, tuviera. Estar: estuvieron, estuviera. Poder: pudieron, pudiera. Hacer: hicieron, hiciera. Decir: dijeron, dijera. Querer: quisieron, quisiera. Saber: supieron, supiera. Poner: pusieron, pusiera. Haber: hubieron, hubiera. Dar: dieron, diera. Ver: vieron, viera. Dormir: durmieron, durmiera. Pedir: pidieron, pidiera. If you know the preterite, you have them all.

There is a second set of endings, -se, -ses, -se, -semos, -seis, -sen (hablase, comiese), used more in Spain and in older writing. You will see it in books and hear it from some speakers. It means the same thing. This course teaches the -ra forms, which are the everyday choice across Latin America and the ones Daniela's grandmother uses.

words.d: the imperfect (past) subjunctive — hablara, comiera, viviera; built from the preterite ellos form
the preterite — the past tense whose ellos form (hablaron, tuvieron, fueron) is the base for the imperfect subjunctive
imperfect subjunctive of ser and ir — from fueron: fuera, fueras, fuera, fuéramos, fuerais, fueran
imperfect subjunctive of tener — from tuvieron: tuviera, tuvieras, tuviera, tuviéramos, tuvierais, tuvieran
imperfect subjunctive of poder — from pudieron: pudiera, pudieras, pudiera, pudiéramos, pudierais, pudieran

look.title: From Preterite to -ra
look.text: Fill the chain for each verb. 1. estar: estuvieron → estuvie- → estuviera, estuvieras, estuviera, estuviéramos, estuvierais, estuvieran. 2. hacer: hicieron → hicie- → hiciera, hicieras, hiciera, hiciéramos, hicierais, hicieran. 3. decir: dijeron → dije- → dijera, dijeras, dijera, dijéramos, dijerais, dijeran. 4. ir: fueron → fue- → fuera. 5. vivir: vivieron → vivie- → viviera.
look.prompt: Now do querer (quisieron), dormir (durmieron) and ver (vieron). Where does the accent go in each nosotros form?

check.q: What is the yo imperfect subjunctive of tener?
check.why: From the preterite tuvieron, drop -ron and add -ra: tuviera. Tenga is present subjunctive, tenía imperfect indicative, tuve preterite.

check.q: Which form belongs to both ser and ir?
check.why: Ser and ir share the preterite fueron, so both have the imperfect subjunctive fuera.

check.q: Where is the accent in the nosotros imperfect subjunctive of hablar?
check.why: The accent falls on the vowel just before -ramos: habláramos. The same pattern gives comiéramos and viviéramos.

lessons.title: Past Triggers, Past Subjunctive
lessons.mainIdea: When the trigger verb is in a past tense, the subjunctive after que shifts to the imperfect subjunctive: quiero que vengas becomes quería que vinieras.
reading: Every trigger from the last chapter still works in the past. The only change is that the subjunctive after que shifts back with it. Present: "Quiero que vengas" (I want you to come). Past: "Quería que vinieras" (I wanted you to come). Present: "Es importante que duermas." Past: "Era importante que durmieras." Present: "Dudo que llegue." Past: "Dudaba que llegara." This matching of tenses is called the *concordancia de tiempos* (sequence of tenses). A present trigger takes the present subjunctive; a past trigger takes the imperfect subjunctive.

The past trigger can be preterite or imperfect. "Mi abuela quería que yo estudiara medicina" (My grandmother wanted me to study medicine). "El maestro nos pidió que escribiéramos un párrafo" (The teacher asked us to write a paragraph). "Me alegré de que vinieran" (I was glad they came). "No creía que fuera posible" (I did not think it was possible). In each case, cover the main clause and you will find an -ra form after que.

Omar tells the class what happened at the town meeting, and the story is full of these. "El alcalde pidió que los jóvenes hablaran primero" (The mayor asked that the young people speak first). "Yo quería que todos me escucharan" (I wanted everyone to listen to me). "Era necesario que alguien dijera la verdad sobre el parque" (It was necessary for someone to tell the truth about the park). "Me sorprendió que tantos vecinos vinieran" (It surprised me that so many neighbors came).

The mistake to watch is mixing the tenses: "Quería que vengas" pairs a past trigger with a present subjunctive, and it sounds wrong to native ears. Match the times, and the sentence will hold together. If the wanting was in the past, the coming is in the imperfect subjunctive too.

words.d: sequence of tenses — a past trigger takes the imperfect subjunctive: quería que vinieras
I wanted (someone) to — Quería que vinieras (I wanted you to come)
he or she asked that — Pidió que habláramos primero (She asked that we speak first)
it was necessary that — Era necesario que alguien dijera la verdad

look.title: Omar Reports Back
look.text: Present version, told before the meeting: Quiero que el alcalde nos escuche. Es importante que todos vengan. Dudo que cambien algo. Past version, told after: Quería que el alcalde nos escuchara. Era importante que todos vinieran. Dudaba que cambiaran algo. (I wanted the mayor to listen to us. It was important that everyone come. I doubted they would change anything.)
look.prompt: Match each present-tense sentence to its past version and name the two verbs that changed. Then move Espero que arreglen el parque into the past.

check.q: Mi abuela quería que yo ___ (estudiar) medicina.
check.why: Quería is a past trigger, so the subjunctive shifts to the imperfect subjunctive estudiara.

check.q: Which sentence correctly matches tenses?
check.why: A past trigger (dudaba) takes the imperfect subjunctive (llegara). Dudaba que llegue mixes past and present, and llega is indicative.

check.q: What does "El maestro nos pidió que escribiéramos un párrafo" mean?
choices: The teacher wrote us a paragraph.
The teacher asked us to write a paragraph.
The teacher asks us to write a paragraph.
We asked the teacher to write a paragraph.
check.why: Pidió is the preterite of pedir, and escribiéramos is the nosotros imperfect subjunctive, so the teacher asked us to write.

lessons.title: The Conditional
lessons.mainIdea: The conditional, formed by adding -ía endings to the whole infinitive, means would, and it shares its irregular stems with the future tense.
reading: Before building the if-sentence from the story, you need its second half. The *condicional* (conditional) is the tense for would. "Cambiaría el parque" means I would change the park. It is one of the easiest tenses to form: keep the whole infinitive and add -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. Hablar: hablaría, hablarías, hablaría, hablaríamos, hablaríais, hablarían. Comer: comería. Vivir: viviría. Every ending carries an accent on the í, and the endings are identical for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.

The conditional uses the same irregular stems as the future tense. *Tener* becomes tendría, *poner* pondría, *salir* saldría, *venir* vendría, *poder* podría, *saber* sabría, *haber* habría, *querer* querría, *hacer* haría, *decir* diría. If you learned "tendré" for I will have, then "tendría" for I would have is the same stem with a different ending. Daniela wrote "pondría más autobuses" (I would put on more buses). That is poner with its irregular stem.

The conditional does three jobs. It says what would happen: "Con más dinero, la ciudad arreglaría las calles" (With more money, the city would fix the streets). It softens a request: "¿Podría hablar con el alcalde?" (Could I speak with the mayor?). And it reports what someone said would happen: "Dijo que vendría" (She said she would come). In this chapter it does the first job, as the partner of the imperfect subjunctive.

Be careful not to confuse the conditional with the imperfect indicative. Comería (I would eat) and comía (I used to eat) look alike, but the conditional keeps the whole infinitive, comer-, in front of the ending. The imperfect drops it: com-ía. Say them side by side and the extra syllable in the conditional stands out.

words.d: the conditional — would: hablaría, comería, viviría; infinitive plus -ía endings
I would change — conditional of cambiar: ¿Qué cambiarías? (What would you change?)
I would put — conditional of poner, irregular stem pondr-: Pondría más autobuses
I could, I would be able to — conditional of poder, stem podr-: ¿Podría hablar con usted?
I would do or make — conditional of hacer, stem har-: ¿Qué harías? (What would you do?)

look.title: One Budget Idea (Example)
rows: Autobús nocturno, un año (night bus, one year)
look.cite: Made-up costs Señora Reyes wrote on the board for a class discussion, not real figures
look.prompt: Using the conditional, say what you would do with 30,000 dollars from this list and why: Con treinta mil dólares, yo… Check every -ía ending and accent.

check.q: What is the yo conditional of tener?
check.why: Tener uses the irregular stem tendr- in both future and conditional: tendría. Tenía is imperfect and tendré is future.

check.q: Which sentence means "I would fix the park"?
check.why: Arreglaría is the conditional, would fix. Arreglo is present, arreglaba is imperfect, arreglaré is future.

check.q: How is the conditional comería different from the imperfect comía?
choices: Comería keeps the whole infinitive comer- before the ending.
check.why: The conditional adds -ía to the full infinitive: comer + ía. The imperfect drops -er first: com + ía.

lessons.title: Si Tuviera, Viajaría
lessons.mainIdea: A contrary-to-fact if-sentence uses si plus the imperfect subjunctive for the condition and the conditional for the result: Si tuviera dinero, viajaría.
reading: Here is the sentence from the board, taken apart. "Si pudieras cambiar una cosa, ¿qué cambiarías?" The si clause holds the condition, and the verb is pudieras, imperfect subjunctive, because the condition is imagined. The other clause holds the result, and the verb is cambiarías, conditional, because it is what would follow. Si plus imperfect subjunctive, then conditional. That is the whole recipe, and it works for every contrary-to-fact sentence in Spanish.

"Si tuviera dinero, viajaría" (If I had money, I would travel). "Si yo fuera alcaldesa, pondría más luces" (If I were mayor, I would put in more lights). "Si la ciudad arreglara el parque, los niños jugarían allí" (If the city fixed the park, the kids would play there). "Si tuviéramos más autobuses, la gente no manejaría tanto" (If we had more buses, people would not drive so much). The order of the two halves can flip: "Viajaría si tuviera dinero." The forms do not change.

Two mistakes to avoid. First, English speakers sometimes put the conditional in both halves, "Si tendría dinero, viajaría," because both feel like would. The si clause never takes the conditional. Second, some learners use the present subjunctive after si, "Si tenga dinero." Si never takes the present subjunctive either. After si, the choice is between the present indicative, for a real possibility, and the imperfect subjunctive, for something imagined.

Daniela's grandmother uses these every day: "Si yo fuera joven, aprendería a manejar" (If I were young, I would learn to drive). "Si tuviera tu edad, estudiaría más" (If I were your age, I would study more). Notice that English also flips to were in "if I were," the one place English still marks this mood. Spanish marks it every time.

words.d: if — no accent; sí with an accent means yes. Si tuviera dinero, viajaría (If I had money, I would travel)
the if-clause — holds the condition; with an imagined condition it takes the imperfect subjunctive
contrary to fact — an imagined condition that is not true now: Si yo fuera alcaldesa (If I were mayor)
I would travel — conditional of viajar, the result of an imagined condition

look.title: Rebuild the Board Sentence
look.text: Start with the pieces. Condition: tener el poder (to have the power). Result: arreglar el parque (to fix the park). Step 1, put the condition after si in the imperfect subjunctive: si tuviera el poder. Step 2, put the result in the conditional: arreglaría el parque. Step 3, join them: Si tuviera el poder, arreglaría el parque. Now try: ser alcalde / poner más luces, and tener más tiempo / ayudar en la biblioteca.
look.prompt: Write both sentences. Then write one about your own town, and check that the si clause is -ra and the result is -ía.

check.q: Si yo ___ (tener) dinero, viajaría a Colombia.
check.why: An imagined condition after si takes the imperfect subjunctive: tuviera. Si never takes the conditional or the present subjunctive.

check.q: Si la ciudad arreglara el parque, los niños ___ (jugar) allí.
check.why: The result of an imagined condition goes in the conditional: jugarían. Jugaran is imperfect subjunctive and belongs only in the si clause.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Si plus imperfect subjunctive (tuviera), then conditional (ayudaría). The other three put the wrong form in one half.

lessons.title: Real If and Imagined If
lessons.mainIdea: Si with the present indicative describes a real possibility and pairs with the present or future; si with the imperfect subjunctive describes something imagined and pairs with the conditional.
reading: Omar's first draft, "Si puedo cambiar una cosa, cambio el parque," was not wrong Spanish. It was the wrong kind of if. Si with the present indicative describes a real, open possibility, and the result goes in the present or the future. "Si llueve, no vamos al parque" (If it rains, we are not going to the park). "Si estudias, vas a aprobar" (If you study, you will pass). "Si tengo tiempo, te llamaré" (If I have time, I will call you). These are conditions that might come true today.

Si with the imperfect subjunctive describes something the speaker treats as unreal, and the result goes in the conditional. "Si lloviera, no iríamos al parque" (If it rained, we would not go to the park), said on a sunny day. "Si estudiaras, aprobarías" (If you studied, you would pass), said to someone who does not. "Si tuviera tiempo, te llamaría" (If I had time, I would call you), meaning I do not. Same si, different mood, different world.

Put the two side by side with the assignment. Real: "Si el alcalde escucha, la ciudad va a cambiar" (If the mayor listens, the city is going to change). Imagined: "Si el alcalde escuchara, la ciudad cambiaría" (If the mayor listened, the city would change). The first speaker thinks it might happen. The second speaker is sure it will not, or is dreaming. Señora Reyes wanted the second kind, because the assignment asks what you would do with a power you do not have.

Omar's final paragraph shows the whole unit at work. "Si pudiera cambiar una cosa, arreglaría el parque para que los niños jugaran sin miedo. Dudo que el alcalde lo haga pronto, pero ojalá que alguien me escuche." (If I could change one thing, I would fix the park so that the kids could play without fear. I doubt the mayor will do it soon, but I hope someone listens to me.) Imperfect subjunctive, conditional, para que with the past subjunctive, doubt, and ojalá, in three lines.

words.d: if with the present indicative — a real possibility: Si llueve, no vamos (If it rains, we are not going)
if with the imperfect subjunctive — imagined: Si lloviera, no iríamos (If it rained, we would not go)
to pass (a test or class) — o→ue: Si estudias, apruebas; Si estudiaras, aprobarías
to listen — Si el alcalde escuchara, la ciudad cambiaría (If the mayor listened, the city would change)

look.title: A Proverb with Aunque
look.text: Aunque la mona se vista de seda, mona se queda. (Even if the monkey dresses in silk, a monkey she stays.) After aunque (even if, although), vista is subjunctive because the dressing is hypothetical, not a report. The proverb means that fancy clothes do not change what someone is.
look.cite: Traditional Spanish proverb, centuries old, author unknown
look.prompt: Why is se vista subjunctive here? How would the meaning change if the proverb said aunque la mona se viste de seda, with the indicative?

check.q: Which sentence describes a real possibility?
check.why: Si with the present indicative (llueve) and a present result (vamos) is a real, open condition. The others use the imperfect subjunctive for imagined ones.

check.q: Si el alcalde ___ (escuchar), la ciudad cambiaría.
check.why: The result cambiaría is conditional, so the condition is imagined and takes the imperfect subjunctive: escuchara.

check.q: What does "Si estudiaras, aprobarías" suggest about the listener?
choices: The listener does not study now.
The listener is going to study tonight.
check.why: The imperfect subjunctive after si presents the condition as contrary to fact: the listener is not studying, or the speaker thinks so.

review.q: Dudo que el alcalde ___ (venir) a la reunión.
review.why: Dudar que expresses doubt and takes the present subjunctive: venga.

review.q: Which conjunction always takes the subjunctive?
review.why: Para que points to a purpose not yet achieved, so it always takes the subjunctive. Porque, así que and ya que report causes and results in the indicative.

review.q: Cuando ___ (llegar) el verano, vamos a nadar en la piscina.
review.why: The main clause points to the future, so cuando takes the present subjunctive: llegue. Llega would describe a habit.

review.q: What is the ellos imperfect subjunctive of decir?
review.why: From the preterite dijeron, drop -ron and add -ran: dijeran. Digan is present subjunctive, decían is imperfect, dijeron is preterite.

review.q: Which sentence correctly follows the sequence of tenses?
review.why: A past trigger, quería, takes the imperfect subjunctive, vinieras. The others mix past and present or use the indicative.

review.q: What is the yo conditional of hacer?
review.why: Hacer uses the irregular stem har- in the conditional: haría. Hacía is imperfect and haré is future.

review.q: Si yo ___ (ser) alcaldesa, pondría más luces en el parque.
review.why: An imagined condition after si takes the imperfect subjunctive: fuera. Si never takes the conditional or the present subjunctive.

review.q: What does "Me alegro de que tantos vecinos vinieran" mean?
choices: I am glad so many neighbors came.
review.why: Alegrarse de que is an emotion trigger, and vinieran is the imperfect subjunctive of venir, so the coming already happened.
